spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad, one row per unique player-referee pair
total dyads in the dataset = 146,028
dyads with skin tone ratings = 124,621 (85.3%)
final analysis sample = 99,937 dyads
light skin dyads = 89,611 (89.7%)
dark skin dyads = 10,326 (10.3%)
red cards observed = 1,242 (1.24%)
unique players = 1,239
unique referees = 2,796
two independent raters coded player skin tone from profile photos on a 5-point scale (0=very light to 1=very dark)
inter-rater reliability r=0.92, described as excellent agreement
averaged the two raters' scores
categorized skin tone as Light (0–0.25), Medium (0.25–0.75), Dark (0.75–1.0)
excluded the medium skin tone category to create a clearer contrast between light and dark
defined a binary exposure variable: Dark skin = 1, Light skin = 0
defined the outcome as a binary indicator of any red card in the player-referee dyad
raw outcome counts: 0 red cards (98.76%), 1 red card (1.22%), 2 red cards (0.02%)
included log(games), the natural log of number of games in the dyad, as a covariate to control for exposure
included yellow cards as a covariate, as a proxy for player aggression/playing style
included league country as a categorical covariate (England, France, Germany, Spain) to control for structural/cultural differences

these covariates address the major confounders: games controls for opportunity, yellow cards proxy for playing style/aggression, and league controls for differences in refereeing standards, bias, and player composition
excluded 21,407 dyads with missing skin tone ratings because no player photo was available
excluded 590 dyads with missing height/weight data, as a sensitivity check
excluded 24,094 dyads with medium skin tone to sharpen the contrast between light and dark
no dyads were excluded due to missing outcome or primary covariate data
applied a natural log transformation to games because its distribution is highly right-skewed (median=1, max=47)
skin tone was averaged across the two raters and then categorized
clustered standard errors by player (playerShort) to account for within-player correlation across multiple dyads
used maximum likelihood logistic regression as the estimation method
calculated the risk difference using average marginal effects (AME), a counterfactual prediction approach
computed confidence intervals via the delta method for marginal effects and Wald intervals for odds ratios
computed p-values via two-sided Wald tests
fitted a logistic model: logit(P(Red Card)) = β0 + β1(Dark Skin) + β2 log(Games) + β3(Yellow Cards) + β4(League)
standard errors were clustered by player
unadjusted risk difference = +0.20 percentage points
chi-square p-value = 0.088, not significant
unadjusted odds ratio = 1.17
the unadjusted analysis shows a pattern similar to the adjusted analysis, suggesting confounding is minimal
